title: Not X, but When: Diagnosing a Mandarin LLM Writing Tic through Contextual Appropriateness

paper.title: Not X , but When: Diagnosing a Mandarin LLM Writing Tic through Contextual Appropriateness
paper.abstract: Abstract Recurring expressions in model-written text are often treated as signatures of machine authorship, yet most of them serve legitimate functions. Whether such an expression is a tic depends on whether the model knows when it is called for. This judgment of appropriateness, central to communicative competence, remains largely unexamined for language models. We study it through the Mandarin corrective construction bushi X, ershi Y (‘not X, but Y’). Drawing on Gricean pragmatics and corrective negation, we introduce a decision tree that classifies uses as substantive, optional, or defective by testing whether the context makes X a live alternative and whether rejecting X is informative. Five commercial models use the construction 2.5 to 9.2 times as densely as a human reference. Of 307 annotated uses, only 1.30% are defective while 52.8% are optional, that is, correct but unneeded, so models fall short in appropriateness far more often than in correctness. Several reward models favor the construction even over quality-matched variants, an LLM judge favors it even where the context does not license it, and both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization tend to raise its frequency in open-weight models. We hope this work encourages the development of models attentive to the appropriateness of their expressions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models can now resolve real-world issues and complete multi-step tasks with tools ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , and a growing share of the text people read is machine-generated. In Grice ’s ( 1975 ) account of cooperative conversation, a contribution should be as informative as the exchange requires and no more, and it should be relevant to the purpose at hand. An entirely accurate response can still fall short of these maxims by elaborating beyond what was asked or by addressing a question that was never at issue. Conformity to these maxims is therefore part of model quality alongside factual accuracy. Figure 1: One form, four discourse functions: substantive ( S S ), unlicensed ( O L O_{L} ), redundant ( O U O_{U} ), and defective ( D D ) uses of not X, but Y . Translated excerpts retain the target sentence; ellipses mark omitted context. Model-written text also contains expressions that recur often enough for readers to treat them as signatures of machine authorship ( Juzek and Ward, 2025 ; Shaib et al., 2025 ) . Most of these expressions are ordinary resources of the language, and human writers use the same devices where the discourse calls for them. Whether a recurring expression amounts to a tic thus depends on whether the model knows when it is called for. Hymes (1972) placed this knowledge at the core of communicative competence, as a judgment of whether an utterance is appropriate to its context, separate from whether it is grammatically possible and from how often it is in fact produced. Research on language models, however, has mostly approached pragmatics from the listener’s side, testing whether models recover implicatures and presuppositions ( Ruis et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Sravanthi et al., 2024 ) , and recent comparisons show that competence in comprehension does not transfer to appropriate production ( Sieker and Zarrieß, 2026 ) . When model production is studied, the usual measure is frequency, with words and phrases that are over-represented relative to human text treated as targets for suppression ( Juzek and Ward, 2025 ; Paech et al., 2025 ) . Frequency answers the last of Hymes’s questions, how often an expression is in fact produced. For expressions with a legitimate function, it conflates appropriate and inappropriate uses, and suppression removes both. Whether models command appropriateness itself remains to be examined. We examine this question through corrective negation, which denies one alternative and asserts another in its place. Its English form, it’s not X, it’s Y , is regularly cited as a hallmark of chatbot writing ( Oremus, 2026 ) , and Chinese online commentary singles out the Mandarin bushi X, ershi Y (‘not X, but Y’; 不是X，而是Y) in the same way, chiefly because the rejected X often appears to be a position that no one has taken. 1 1 1 For example, https://blog.darkthread.net/blog/ai-slop-not-but-pattern/ . Corrective negation is also the ordinary way to correct a misconception. Each use of the construction thus raises the two questions behind Grice’s maxims (Figure 1 ): whether the context made X a live alternative (relevance), and whether rejecting X contributes information not already established (quantity). We ask whether models, like competent speakers, know when the construction is called for. Linguistic theory makes these questions precise as conditions on licensing. As a construction, bushi X, ershi Y conventionally pairs its form with a corrective function ( Goldberg, 2006 ; Shao and Wang, 2010 ; Zuo, 2025 ) . The correction presupposes alternatives that contrast along a shared dimension ( Rooth, 1992 ) , and X need not have been asserted by anyone as long as it is accessible in the common ground ( Toosarvandani, 2013 ; Stalnaker, 2002 ) . What is rejected may be a proposition or the manner in which it is expressed, as in metalinguistic negation ( Horn, 1985 ) , and whether the correction is informative depends on the question under discussion ( Roberts, 2012 ) . These accounts separate three cases that are formally identical: a correction that resolves a live alternative, one that is well formed but unneeded, and one that is defective because it rejects something true or misattributes a view. We introduce a diagnostic framework built around an ordered decision tree (Figure 2 ) that sorts each use of the construction into these three cases, first screening out defective uses and then testing the relevance and quantity conditions; a use that passes both is substantive, and one that fails either is optional. We apply the tree to answers from five commercial models on Chinese prompts and compare their usage with a human reference. We then investigate the sources of this preference, scoring each answer against minimally edited counterparts with reward models and an LLM judge, and tracing the construction’s frequency across training stages of open-weight models and in public preference data. For a substantial share of uses, models do not. They use the construction 2.5 to 9.2 times as densely as the human reference, and the shortfall lies in appropriateness more than in correctness, with only 1.30% of annotated uses defective and 52.8% classified as optional. Several reward models favor the construction even when variants match in general quality, and an LLM judge favors it even where the context does not license it. Along the training pipelines of open-weight models, both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization tend to raise its frequency. Our contributions are as follows: • We formalize stylistic tics in LLM-generated text as a failure of appropriateness in the sense of communicative competence. • We distinguish uses that are correct from uses that are needed, and operationalize this distinction as a decision tree derived from linguistic theory. • We provide a method for diagnosing how reward models and training stages shape the preference for such expressions.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Our work draws on three lines of research. Studies of language models as speakers identify which expressions models overproduce; linguistic accounts of corrective negation specify when the construction is appropriate; and work on evaluator bias suggests where a preference for it may originate.

sections.heading: 2.1 Language Models as Speakers
sections.text: Research on language models has examined their pragmatic competence and their characteristic output largely in isolation. Pragmatic evaluations have mostly taken the listener’s side, testing whether models recover implicatures and presuppositions ( Ruis et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Sravanthi et al., 2024 ) or recognize constructional meaning ( Weissweiler et al., 2022 ) . The speaker’s side has a longer history in generation, where Gricean maxims constrain referring expressions ( Dale and Reiter, 1995 ) and pragmatic speakers reason about a listener in reference games ( Frank and Goodman, 2012 ; Andreas and Klein, 2016 ) , though in tasks whose communicative goal is fixed in advance. Studies of open-ended model writing instead focus on its characteristic expressions, including over-represented words ( Juzek and Ward, 2025 ; Kobak et al., 2025 ) , recurring syntactic templates ( Shaib et al., 2024 ) , and broader measures of low-quality “slop” ( Shaib et al., 2025 ) , with suppression proposed as a remedy ( Paech et al., 2025 ) . These studies establish which expressions models produce too often, which is a matter of frequency.

sections.heading: 2.2 Corrective Negation
sections.text: Corrective negation is well described in both English and Mandarin, and these descriptions specify when a speaker uses it appropriately. The construction denies one alternative and asserts another in its place. Work on English shows that it presupposes alternatives contrasting along a shared dimension and can target the form of an utterance as well as its content ( Horn, 1985 ; Toosarvandani, 2013 ) . Studies of bushi … ershi describe the same corrective function in Mandarin. Shao and Wang (2010) identify a pseudo-denial use, in which the negation does not retract any claim held in the context; Tan (2016) compares the construction with English not A but B and finds both semantic and metalinguistic correction in each; and Zuo (2025) analyzes ershi as the connective that lexicalizes correction, distinct from those for contrast and adversative relations. We turn these descriptions into conditions for assessing each use in model output.

sections.heading: 2.3 Evaluator Bias
sections.text: The evaluators used to train and assess language models are biased toward surface features of responses, and training can carry these biases into model output. Reward models and LLM judges favor longer responses ( Singhal et al., 2024 ) , list formatting ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and style more broadly ( Wu and Aji, 2025 ) , and LLM judges show position and verbosity biases ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . Preference optimization also narrows the range of model outputs ( Kirk et al., 2024 ) , and open post-training pipelines that release intermediate checkpoints make it possible to trace such changes stage by stage ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; OLMo et al., 2025 ) . Unlike length or formatting, a corrective construction’s appropriateness depends on context; the question is whether evaluators and training favor it only where it is called for. sections.heading: 3 Methods
sections.text: We propose a diagnostic framework that assesses each use of the construction by whether its context calls for it, rather than by how often it occurs. Its core is a decision tree, derived from corrective negation and Gricean pragmatics, that labels each occurrence as substantive, optional, or defective. We pair these labels with frequency measures, evaluator comparisons, and checkpoint analyses to trace the sources of the preference.

sections.heading: 3.1 Analytical Criteria
sections.text: We operationalize contextual appropriateness through corrective meaning and discourse contribution. A descriptive reading approximates ¬ p X ∧ p Y \neg p_{X}\land p_{Y} ; metalinguistic negation rejects wording or degree ( Horn, 1985 ) , while reframing replaces an explanatory perspective. Alternatives share a recoverable contrast dimension ( Rooth, 1992 ; Toosarvandani, 2013 ) , and their availability differs from a participant’s endorsement ( Stalnaker, 2002 ) . Grice’s Relation and Quantity maxims motivate separate tests of contextual licensing and informative contribution; Manner motivates checking interpretability ( Grice, 1975 ) . We assess contribution against the current question under discussion (QUD), which tracks the distinctions still open in the discourse ( Roberts, 2012 ) . For instance, the bottleneck is not the CPU, but disk I/O is licensed and informative when the user reports that upgrading the CPU did not help; it is unlicensed when nothing has raised the CPU, and redundant when the answer has already ruled the CPU out.

sections.heading: 3.2 An Evidence-Based Diagnostic Tree
sections.text: The unit is one occurrence in its complete answer and available context. Annotators recover X/Y, reading, scope, commitment holder, and QUD, then follow Figure 2 , citing evidence at each visited node.

sections.heading: Detect established defects: T → \rightarrow A → \rightarrow P.
sections.text: T tests for factual conflict, contradiction, or invalid exclusion under the recovered reading. A tests whether the correction misattributes a position. P tests for inappropriate rejection or disrupted interpretation, requiring a target signal, an independent defect basis, and a specific consequence, such as obstructed reference or unjustified issue replacement. Missing motivation alone is assessed at L. The first positive finding assigns D (defective) .

sections.heading: Assess corrective function: R → \rightarrow L → \rightarrow U.
sections.text: For remaining occurrences, R asks whether X/Y express a recoverable rejection and replacement. L requires a concrete contextual cue motivating the exclusion of X, independently of the contrast itself. U asks whether the correction advances an open distinction, supplies a missing replacement, or repairs a commitment under the QUD. Restating a completed correction fails U. The first negative answer assigns O (optional) , subtyped O R O_{R} , O L O_{L} , or O U O_{U} ; passing all three assigns S (substantive) . Annotators receive the original response without edited variants, evaluator scores, source identity, or prior labels. Factual status and confidence are recorded separately.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments address two questions: whether models use the construction where it is called for, and where their preference for it comes from. We answer the first by comparing model and human usage in frequency and function, and the second by examining evaluator preferences, training stages, and public preference data.

sections.heading: Comparison.
sections.text: We examine 5,285 answers from five API models—GPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, GLM, and Qwen—to 1,061 Chinese prompts drawn from AlignBench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , WritingBench ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , COIG-CQIA ( Bai et al., 2024 ) , and Arena-Hard-v2 ( LMArena, 2026 ) . A human reference comprises community answers, examination responses, student essays, and role-play dialogue. We compare construction density per 10,000 Han characters, averaging equally over four shared task dimensions: professional ability, general question answering, Chinese understanding, and writing. sections.heading: Models repeatedly select the construction.
sections.text: Across the five models, density is 2.5–9.2 times the human reference (Figure 3 a). The human reference answers different prompts, and its detector also admits comma-free and cross-sentence forms that the model detector excludes; this detection difference, if anything, understates the gap. The construction is thus a recurrent choice across models, rather than a peculiarity of one system. Its local contribution is a separate question: frequent corrections may resolve an outstanding alternative, but they may also introduce a contrast the answer does not need.

sections.heading: Many corrections lack a substantive corrective function.
sections.text: Of 308 selected occurrences, one cybersecurity-related item triggered a refusal from the Claude annotation service and yielded no valid label, leaving 307 occurrences for functional analysis in their full context. Labels were generated with claude-sonnet-5-5 and subsequently audited. Optional uses account for 52.8% of the 307 annotated cases (Figure 3 b,c; Table 4 ). Contextual licensing or issue advancement accounts for 96.4% of non-substantive decisions. The recurring problem is thus a correction introduced without a contextual reason, or repeated after its work has already been done. Only four occurrences are classified as defective.

sections.heading: Human-authored uses are more often substantive.
sections.text: We apply the same tree to the human reference. Of its 38 detected occurrences, five are quoted or metalinguistic and are excluded before tree application. Among the remaining 33, 63.6% are substantive and 33.3% optional, compared with 45.9% and 52.8% in model answers (Figure 3 c). The difference is concentrated in unlicensed uses (12.1% vs. 24.1%); redundant uses differ less (21.2% vs. 28.0%). Models therefore not only use the construction more densely, but a larger share of their uses introduces an alternative that the context gives no reason to reject (Appendix A.1 ).

sections.heading: Reward preference extends to optional corrections.
sections.text: FsfairX ( Dong et al., 2024 ) , Skywork ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and OffsetBias ( Park et al., 2024 ) prefer the original order in 68.3–76.8% of non-tied optional-use comparisons (Figure 4 a). ArmoRM ( Wang et al., 2024 ) shows a weaker preference, whereas InternLM2 ( Cai et al., 2024 ) favors the reordered version. The result identifies a recurring preference in three evaluators: they reward the original realization even where the tree classifies the correction as optional.

sections.heading: Judges favor retaining unlicensed corrections.
sections.text: For corrections without contextual licensing, Claude Sonnet 5.5 prefers the original over the affirmative-only answer (mean score 0.630) and over reordering (0.563; Figure 4 c; Table 7 ). GPT-6.1-sol shows weaker but directionally consistent preferences (0.519 and 0.517, respectively). Critically, neither judge’s preference varies with corrective function: substantive-minus-unlicensed differences are 0.002 and 0.005 for Claude, and − 0.002 -0.002 and − 0.001 -0.001 for GPT; all four 95% intervals include zero (Figure 4 d). This insensitivity indicates that both judges reward the construction’s surface form regardless of whether the context licenses it.

sections.heading: Ordering preference persists under quality-score matching.
sections.text: To examine whether reward models’ preference for the original order is associated with general answer quality, we retain original–reordered pairs with identical scores on every applicable quality dimension. Excluding reward-model ties, FsfairX, Skywork, and OffsetBias still prefer “not X, but Y” over “Y, not X” in 73.1–78.3% of comparisons (Table 6 ). Thus, these three reward models exhibit an ordering preference even when the quality scores do not distinguish the two versions.

sections.heading: Open checkpoints use the construction less frequently than API models.
sections.text: Across the four shared task dimensions, open-checkpoint density ranges from 0 to 1.41 occurrences per 10,000 Han characters, compared with 0.942 for the human reference and 2.38–8.68 for the API models (Figure 5 a). Ten of the twelve open checkpoints fall below 0.500. The high-frequency pattern is therefore concentrated in the API cohort rather than shared by the selected open checkpoints.

sections.heading: Density rises across the displayed SFT and DPO stages.
sections.text: Under the four-benchmark Unicode measure, all five families have higher construction density at SFT than at Base. Both available DPO checkpoints also exceed their SFT predecessors, reaching the highest density within the displayed trajectories (Figure 5 b). Paired density changes on common successful prompts are also positive for all seven transitions (Table 8 ). These descriptive patterns associate SFT and DPO with increased use of the construction in this checkpoint panel.

sections.heading: Preferred training answers more often contain the construction.
sections.text: In public preference data, chosen answers activate the construction more often than rejected answers in both datasets: +14.7% relative activation in Tülu 3 and +26.5% in OLMo 2 (Table 9 ). The direction is consistent across datasets and the gap is larger in OLMo 2. Both Han-content subsets in each corpus also show higher chosen-answer density. This enrichment is directionally consistent with the displayed DPO increases. Its magnitude depends on corpus composition and repetition.

sections.heading: 4.4 Case Study
sections.text: Table 1 presents two sports answers differing mainly in whether context supplies X. In a victory speech by a swimmer long troubled by injury, the finish is what a new champion would naturally recall, and the injury motivates setting it aside. In commentary on Messi’s World Cup title, no one suggests that the title amounts merely to winning; the target raises this view only to reject it, although winning the final is precisely what the title is. Yet the LLM judge favors the original in every judgment for both answers except one tie. For Messi, it concedes that the sentence is “slightly odd logically” and still prefers it because it “reads smoothly and passionately.” FsfairX and Skywork also score the original above the reordered version in both cases. The evaluators reward the construction’s rhetorical effect, not whether the context raises the rejected alternative.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: Frequency and appropriateness are separate properties of model usage. Models produce the construction far more often than people do, and many of these uses are correct but not called for. Evaluators do not supply the missing judgment: several reward models prefer the construction after general-quality matching, and both judges prefer it within unlicensed uses. In the available checkpoints, its density also rises through SFT and DPO. Suppressing the form would remove its appropriate uses along with the rest; reducing tics of this kind requires evaluation and training signals that register whether an expression is called for. The diagnostic is not specific to Mandarin: screening for defects and then testing contextual licensing and issue advancement can be applied to English it’s not X, it’s Y and to other expressions that are legitimate in some contexts and overused in others. A controlled follow-up can test this attribution by holding SFT initialization, source composition, update budget, and prompts fixed, intervening on construction-bearing preference pairs with matched edits, and repeating training across seeds. Measuring activation, repetition, and local function would then separate changes in how often the construction is selected from changes in what it contributes.

sections.heading: Data coverage.
sections.text: Our analysis covers five commercial models, a limited set of task domains, and 307 annotated uses. Broader models, domains, and human data would strengthen the estimates.

sections.heading: Observational training evidence.
sections.text: The checkpoint and preference-data comparisons are observational, so they show that frequency rises along training pipelines but do not establish which stage or data causes the rise. Controlled retraining is needed to test this attribution.

sections.heading: Reader perception.
sections.text: We assess appropriateness through linguistic criteria and do not measure how readers perceive the construction. Whether unneeded uses cause annoyance or affect comprehension requires a separate user study.

sections.heading: Languages and constructions.
sections.text: We study a single Mandarin construction. Although the decision tree is designed to transfer to English it’s not X, it’s Y and other recurring expressions, we have not applied it beyond bushi X, ershi Y .

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: This section discusses the ethical considerations and broader impact of this work.

sections.heading: Potential Risks.
sections.text: The decision tree describes when a corrective construction is called for, and this description could be used to make model-written text resemble human writing more closely and thus harder to identify. Conversely, the frequency measures could be misread as evidence of machine authorship and applied to judge human writers, who also use the construction. Our analyses concern aggregate usage across models and corpora; they are not designed or validated for attributing individual texts to humans or machines.

sections.heading: Intellectual Property.
sections.text: The benchmarks, open-weight checkpoints, reward models, and preference mixtures used in this work are publicly released for research, and we use them in accordance with their respective licenses. Commercial models are accessed through their official APIs under the providers’ terms of service. All materials are used solely for scientific research.

sections.heading: Data Privacy.
sections.text: The human reference is drawn from publicly available datasets, and personally identifiable information was removed before analysis. Model answers are generated from public benchmark prompts. The human annotators are students with a background in linguistics who participated voluntarily; no personal information about them is collected beyond their annotations.

sections.heading: Intended Use.
sections.text: The diagnostic framework is intended for analyzing contextual appropriateness in model-generated text and for examining how evaluators and training stages shape such usage. It is not intended for authorship detection or for evaluating individual writers.

sections.heading: Documentation of Artifacts.
sections.text: We will release our code and the annotation guidelines for the decision tree. Both are documented with respect to their scope: the Mandarin construction bushi X, ershi Y , the task domains covered, and the procedures described in Appendices A – D .

sections.heading: AI Assistants in Research or Writing.
sections.text: We use Cursor for code development assistance and a large language model for refining and polishing the language of the paper. The use of language models as annotators and judges is part of the method and is described in Section 3 and Appendices A.1 and B .

sections.heading: Human-reference sources.
sections.text: The human baseline draws on cMedQA2 for medical community question–answer pairs; HC3 for Chinese human answers on finance, law, psychology, and everyday topics; and COIG for Chinese-language examination answers and explanations. The Chinese Essay Dataset supplies student essays in six genres, and CrossWOZ supplies travel-assistant dialogues role-played by human participants. We also use worked solutions for the 2016–2018 management entrance examinations hosted by China University of Petroleum (East China) , solutions for the 2020 examination hosted by Shanghai Normal University , and reference answers for the 2020 independent-admission mathematics examination hosted by the High School Affiliated to Anhui Normal University .

sections.heading: Corpora and generation.
sections.text: The human reference contains 572,412 Han characters and 38 occurrences across eight dimensions. The main comparison gives equal weight to the four dimensions represented by these occurrences: professional ability, general question answering, Chinese understanding, and writing. Han exposure counts code points in U+4E00--U+9FFF . The four-dimension mean is .942 occurrences per 10,000 Han characters; pooling all eight human dimensions gives .664. Human materials allow comma-free and cross-sentence realizations, whereas the model detector requires a comma. The model panel contains 683 AlignBench, 100 WritingBench, 200 COIG-CQIA, and 78 Arena-Hard-v2 prompts. The five logged model identifiers are gpt-5.6-luna , deepseek-v4.1-flash , gemini-3.8-flash , glm-5.3-flash , and qwen3.8-flash . sections.heading: Detection and frequency measures.
sections.text: The fixed detector finds non-overlapping literal matches, permits an optional preceding bing , requires a Chinese or ASCII comma before ershi , and limits the captured alternatives to 160 and 220 characters. Slots exclude sentence-final punctuation, semicolons, and newlines; intervening whitespace may span a newline. Nested starts and comma-free forms can be missed, and interrogative strings can produce spurious detections. For valid answer i i , let c i c_{i} count occurrences and ℓ i ( u ) \ell_{i}^{(u)} count Han or all Unicode characters. sections.heading: A.1 Functional Annotation and Human Comparison
sections.text: The sample comprises 308 selected response groups. One cybersecurity-related item triggered a refusal from the Claude annotation service and yielded no valid label; the functional analysis therefore covers 307 annotated targets. Labels were generated with claude-sonnet-5-5 and subsequently audited. Annotation excludes templates, purely metalinguistic quoted strings, and known incomplete materials. Annotators assess the original response without edited variants or evaluator scores, recover the supported reading and question under discussion, and record factual uncertainty separately. An implicit question under discussion requires contextual evidence independent of the target contrast. The annotated sample contains 141 substantive, 162 optional, and four defective uses (Table 4 ). Optional uses comprise 52.8% of all 307 annotated cases and 53.5% of the 303 non-defective cases. Figure 3 b,c includes all classified cases. sections.heading: Agreement with the human annotations.
sections.text: We compare annotations from two independent human annotators, both with a background in linguistics, on the same 100 cases (Table 5 ). We report exact agreement and unweighted Cohen’s κ \kappa for the top-level outcomes (S/O/D) and the seven terminal labels (S, R, L, U, T, A, P). Terminal-label agreement requires the full classification, including the subtype when applicable, to match. Both annotators labeled the cases independently without consensus discussion. The κ \kappa values indicate moderate agreement ( Landis and Koch, 1977 ) . The expected drop at the terminal level reflects the inherent difficulty of distinguishing fine-grained pragmatic subcategories (e.g., O L O_{L} vs. O U O_{U} ), even for trained linguists. sections.heading: Human-authored functional baseline.
sections.text: The human corpus contains 38 detected occurrences. After excluding five quoted or metalinguistic instances before tree application, Codex classifies 33 eligible occurrences under the same protocol: 21 substantive, four unlicensed, seven redundant, and one defective. These labels did not undergo the review applied to the model sample. Section 4.1 compares them with the model sample. They are automated annotations of human-authored text and are distinct from the human raters described above.

sections.heading: Discourse position.
sections.text: Target position is its first start index divided by answer length. Median positions are 0.341 for substantive corrections, 0.544 for unlicensed corrections, and 0.862 for redundant corrections. The substantive–unlicensed difference has p < .001 p<.001 . Summary cues occur before 7.80%, 14.9%, and 32.6% of these targets. Both optional subtypes occur later than substantive corrections. These associations are descriptive and do not enter the evaluator tests.

sections.heading: Variants and reward models.
sections.text: Each selected response yields four variants. For compatibility with the released data, A denotes the original, B the reordered version, C a cross-sentence version, and D the affirmative-only version. The main text uses the first, second, and fourth. The cross-sentence variant is not used in the reported comparisons. ArmoRM-8B, FsfairX-8B, InternLM2-7B-Reward, OffsetBias-8B, and Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-8B receive the question and full answer without functional or variant labels. Overlength inputs are excluded. The first, second, and fourth scorers cover 252 complete groups; InternLM2 and Skywork cover 305. Their common intersection contains 252 groups. The scoring release preserves all originals and repairs 67 edited variants in 35 groups. Mean reward contrasts are standardized by the original-answer score standard deviation. Functional-sensitivity intervals use 10,000 item bootstraps.

sections.heading: General-quality matching.
sections.text: The numerical-quality rubric contains 24 general dimensions. Matching requires unchanged scored texts and equal scores on every applicable dimension, excluding the construction-clarity manipulation check. Affiliation: Tsinghua University Abstract Recurring expressions in model-written text are often treated as signatures of machine authorship, yet most of them serve legitimate functions. Whether such an expression is a tic depends on whether the model knows when it is called for. This judgment of appropriateness, central to communicative competence, remains largely unexamined for language models. We study it through the Mandarin corrective construction bushi X, ershi Y (‘not X, but Y’). Drawing on Gricean pragmatics and corrective negation, we introduce a decision tree that classifies uses as substantive, optional, or defective by testing whether the context makes X a live alternative and whether rejecting X is informative. Five commercial models use the construction 2.5 to 9.2 times as densely as a human reference. Of 307 annotated uses, only 1.30% are defective while 52.8% are optional, that is, correct but unneeded, so models fall short in appropriateness far more often than in correctness. Several reward models favor the construction even over quality-matched variants, an LLM judge favors it even where the context does not license it, and both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization tend to raise its frequency in open-weight models. We hope this work encourages the development of models attentive to the appropriateness of their expressions. 1 Introduction Large language models can now resolve real-world issues and complete multi-step tasks with tools ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) , and a growing share of the text people read is machine-generated. In Grice ’s ( 1975 ) account of cooperative conversation, a contribution should be as informative as the exchange requires and no more, and it should be relevant to the purpose at hand. An entirely accurate response can still fall short of these maxims by elaborating beyond what was asked or by addressing a question that was never at issue. Conformity to these maxims is therefore part of model quality alongside factual accuracy. Figure 1: One form, four discourse functions: substantive ( S S ), unlicensed ( O L O_{L} ), redundant ( O U O_{U} ), and defective ( D D ) uses of not X, but Y . Translated excerpts retain the target sentence; ellipses mark omitted context. Model-written text also contains expressions that recur often enough for readers to treat them as signatures of machine authorship ( Juzek and Ward, 2025 ; Shaib et al., 2025 ) . Most of these expressions are ordinary resources of the language, and human writers use the same devices where the discourse calls for them. Whether a recurring expression amounts to a tic thus depends on whether the model knows when it is called for. Hymes (1972) placed this knowledge at the core of communicative competence, as a judgment of whether an utterance is appropriate to its context, separate from whether it is grammatically possible and from how often it is in fact produced. Research on language models, however, has mostly approached pragmatics from the listener’s side, testing whether models recover implicatures and presuppositions ( Ruis et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Sravanthi et al., 2024 ) , and recent comparisons show that competence in comprehension does not transfer to appropriate production ( Sieker and Zarrieß, 2026 ) . When model production is studied, the usual measure is frequency, with words and phrases that are over-represented relative to human text treated as targets for suppression ( Juzek and Ward, 2025 ; Paech et al., 2025 ) . Frequency answers the last of Hymes’s questions, how often an expression is in fact produced. For expressions with a legitimate function, it conflates appropriate and inappropriate uses, and suppression removes both. Whether models command appropriateness itself remains to be examined. We examine this question through corrective negation, which denies one alternative and asserts another in its place. Its English form, it’s not X, it’s Y , is regularly cited as a hallmark of chatbot writing ( Oremus, 2026 ) , and Chinese online commentary singles out the Mandarin bushi X, ershi Y (‘not X, but Y’; 不是X，而是Y) in the same way, chiefly because the rejected X often appears to be a position that no one has taken. 1 1 1 For example, https://blog.darkthread.net/blog/ai-slop-not-but-pattern/ . Corrective negation is also the ordinary way to correct a misconception. Each use of the construction thus raises the two questions behind Grice’s maxims (Figure 1 ): whether the context made X a live alternative (relevance), and whether rejecting X contributes information not already established (quantity). We ask whether models, like competent speakers, know when the construction is called for. Linguistic theory makes these questions precise as conditions on licensing. As a construction, bushi X, ershi Y conventionally pairs its form with a corrective function ( Goldberg, 2006 ; Shao and Wang, 2010 ; Zuo, 2025 ) . The correction presupposes alternatives that contrast along a shared dimension ( Rooth, 1992 ) , and X need not have been asserted by anyone as long as it is accessible in the common ground ( Toosarvandani, 2013 ; Stalnaker, 2002 ) . What is rejected may be a proposition or the manner in which it is expressed, as in metalinguistic negation ( Horn, 1985 ) , and whether the correction is informative depends on the question under discussion ( Roberts, 2012 ) . These accounts separate three cases that are formally identical: a correction that resolves a live alternative, one that is well formed but unneeded, and one that is defective because it rejects something true or misattributes a view. We introduce a diagnostic framework built around an ordered decision tree (Figure 2 ) that sorts each use of the construction into these three cases, first screening out defective uses and then testing the relevance and quantity conditions; a use that passes both is substantive, and one that fails either is optional. We apply the tree to answers from five commercial models on Chinese prompts and compare their usage with a human reference. We then investigate the sources of this preference, scoring each answer against minimally edited counterparts with reward models and an LLM judge, and tracing the construction’s frequency across training stages of open-weight models and in public preference data. For a substantial share of uses, models do not. They use the construction 2.5 to 9.2 times as densely as the human reference, and the shortfall lies in appropriateness more than in correctness, with only 1.30% of annotated uses defective and 52.8% classified as optional. Several reward models favor the construction even when variants match in general quality, and an LLM judge favors it even where the context does not license it. Along the training pipelines of open-weight models, both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization tend to raise its frequency. Our contributions are as follows: • We formalize stylistic tics in LLM-generated text as a failure of appropriateness in the sense of communicative competence. • We distinguish uses that are correct from uses that are needed, and operationalize this distinction as a decision tree derived from linguistic theory. • We provide a method for diagnosing how reward models and training stages shape the preference for such expressions. 2 Related Work Our work draws on three lines of research. Studies of language models as speakers identify which expressions models overproduce; linguistic accounts of corrective negation specify when the construction is appropriate; and work on evaluator bias suggests where a preference for it may originate. 2.1 Language Models as Speakers Research on language models has examined their pragmatic competence and their characteristic output largely in isolation. Pragmatic evaluations have mostly taken the listener’s side, testing whether models recover implicatures and presuppositions ( Ruis et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Sravanthi et al., 2024 ) or recognize constructional meaning ( Weissweiler et al., 2022 ) . The speaker’s side has a longer history in generation, where Gricean maxims constrain referring expressions ( Dale and Reiter, 1995 ) and pragmatic speakers reason about a listener in reference games ( Frank and Goodman, 2012 ; Andreas and Klein, 2016 ) , though in tasks whose communicative goal is fixed in advance. Studies of open-ended model writing instead focus on its characteristic expressions, including over-represented words ( Juzek and Ward, 2025 ; Kobak et al., 2025 ) , recurring syntactic templates ( Shaib et al., 2024 ) , and broader measures of low-quality “slop” ( Shaib et al., 2025 ) , with suppression proposed as a remedy ( Paech et al., 2025 ) . These studies establish which expressions models produce too often, which is a matter of frequency. 2.2 Corrective Negation Corrective negation is well described in both English and Mandarin, and these descriptions specify when a speaker uses it appropriately. The construction denies one alternative and asserts another in its place. Work on English shows that it presupposes alternatives contrasting along a shared dimension and can target the form of an utterance as well as its content ( Horn, 1985 ; Toosarvandani, 2013 ) . Studies of bushi … ershi describe the same corrective function in Mandarin. Shao and Wang (2010) identify a pseudo-denial use, in which the negation does not retract any claim held in the context; Tan (2016) compares the construction with English not A but B and finds both semantic and metalinguistic correction in each; and Zuo (2025) analyzes ershi as the connective that lexicalizes correction, distinct from those for contrast and adversative relations. We turn these descriptions into conditions for assessing each use in model output. 2.3 Evaluator Bias The evaluators used to train and assess language models are biased toward surface features of responses, and training can carry these biases into model output. Reward models and LLM judges favor longer responses ( Singhal et al., 2024 ) , list formatting ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and style more broadly ( Wu and Aji, 2025 ) , and LLM judges show position and verbosity biases ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . Preference optimization also narrows the range of model outputs ( Kirk et al., 2024 ) , and open post-training pipelines that release intermediate checkpoints make it possible to trace such changes stage by stage ( Lambert et al., 2024 ; OLMo et al., 2025 ) . Unlike length or formatting, a corrective construction’s appropriateness depends on context; the question is whether evaluators and training favor it only where it is called for. Figure 2: Diagnostic tree and experimental framework. (a) Recover the contextual reading, then test defects (T/A/P) and corrective function (R/L/U). (b) Connect generation patterns to evaluator preferences, checkpoint trajectories, and preference-data composition. 3 Methods We propose a diagnostic framework that assesses each use of the construction by whether its context calls for it, rather than by how often it occurs. Its core is a decision tree, derived from corrective negation and Gricean pragmatics, that labels each occurrence as substantive, optional, or defective. We pair these labels with frequency measures, evaluator comparisons, and checkpoint analyses to trace the sources of the preference. 3.1 Analytical Criteria We operationalize contextual appropriateness through corrective meaning and discourse contribution. A descriptive reading approximates ¬ p X ∧ p Y \neg p_{X}\land p_{Y} ; metalinguistic negation rejects wording or degree ( Horn, 1985 ) , while reframing replaces an explanatory perspective. Alternatives share a recoverable contrast dimension ( Rooth, 1992 ; Toosarvandani, 2013 ) , and their availability differs from a participant’s endorsement ( Stalnaker, 2002 ) . Grice’s Relation and Quantity maxims motivate separate tests of contextual licensing and informative contribution; Manner motivates checking interpretability ( Grice, 1975 ) . We assess contribution against the current question under discussion (QUD), which tracks the distinctions still open in the discourse ( Roberts, 2012 ) . For instance, the bottleneck is not the CPU, but disk I/O is licensed and informative when the user reports that upgrading the CPU did not help; it is unlicensed when nothing has raised the CPU, and redundant when the answer has already ruled the CPU out. 3.2 An Evidence-Based Diagnostic Tree The unit is one occurrence in its complete answer and available context. Annotators recover X/Y, reading, scope, commitment holder, and QUD, then follow Figure 2 , citing evidence at each visited node. Detect established defects: T → \rightarrow A → \rightarrow P. T tests for factual conflict, contradiction, or invalid exclusion under the recovered reading. A tests whether the correction misattributes a position. P tests for inappropriate rejection or disrupted interpretation, requiring a target signal, an independent defect basis, and a specific consequence, such as obstructed reference or unjustified issue replacement. Missing motivation alone is assessed at L. The first positive finding assigns D (defective) . Assess corrective function: R → \rightarrow L → \rightarrow U. For remaining occurrences, R asks whether X/Y express a recoverable rejection and replacement. L requires a concrete contextual cue motivating the exclusion of X, independently of the contrast itself. U asks whether the correction advances an open distinction, supplies a missing replacement, or repairs a commitment under the QUD. Restating a completed correction fails U. The first negative answer assigns O (optional) , subtyped O R O_{R} , O L O_{L} , or O U O_{U} ; passing all three assigns S (substantive) . Annotators receive the original response without edited variants, evaluator scores, source identity, or prior labels. We answer the first by comparing model and human usage in frequency and function, and the second by examining evaluator preferences, training stages, and public preference data. 4.1 Frequency and Function Comparison. We examine 5,285 answers from five API models—GPT, DeepSeek, Gemini, GLM, and Qwen—to 1,061 Chinese prompts drawn from AlignBench ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , WritingBench ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , COIG-CQIA ( Bai et al., 2024 ) , and Arena-Hard-v2 ( LMArena, 2026 ) . Reward preference extends to optional corrections. FsfairX ( Dong et al., 2024 ) , Skywork ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and OffsetBias ( Park et al., 2024 ) prefer the original order in 68.3–76.8% of non-tied optional-use comparisons (Figure 4 a). To examine whether reward models’ preference for the original order is associated with general answer quality, we retain original–reordered pairs with identical scores on every applicable quality dimension. In a victory speech by a swimmer long troubled by injury, the finish is what a new champion would naturally recall, and the injury motivates setting it aside. In commentary on Messi’s World Cup title, no one suggests that the title amounts merely to winning; the target raises this view only to reject it, although winning the final is precisely what the title is. Yet the LLM judge favors the original in every judgment for both answers except one tie. For Messi, it concedes that the sentence is “slightly odd logically” and still prefers it because it “reads smoothly and passionately.” FsfairX and Skywork also score the original above the reordered version in both cases. The evaluators reward the construction’s rhetorical effect, not whether the context raises the rejected alternative. 5 Discussion and Conclusion Frequency and appropriateness are separate properties of model usage. Models produce the construction far more often than people do, and many of these uses are correct but not called for. Evaluators do not supply the missing judgment: several reward models prefer the construction after general-quality matching, and both judges prefer it within unlicensed uses. In the available checkpoints, its density also rises through SFT and DPO. Suppressing the form would remove its appropriate uses along with the rest; reducing tics of this kind requires evaluation and training signals that register whether an expression is called for. The diagnostic is not specific to Mandarin: screening for defects and then testing contextual licensing and issue advancement can be applied to English it’s not X, it’s Y and to other expressions that are legitimate in some contexts and overused in others. A controlled follow-up can test this attribution by holding SFT initialization, source composition, update budget, and prompts fixed, intervening on construction-bearing preference pairs with matched edits, and repeating training across seeds. Measuring activation, repetition, and local function would then separate changes in how often the construction is selected from changes in what it contributes. Limitations Data coverage. Our analysis covers five commercial models, a limited set of task domains, and 307 annotated uses. Broader models, domains, and human data would strengthen the estimates. Observational training evidence. The checkpoint and preference-data comparisons are observational, so they show that frequency rises along training pipelines but do not establish which stage or data causes the rise. Controlled retraining is needed to test this attribution. Reader perception. We assess appropriateness through linguistic criteria and do not measure how readers perceive the construction. Whether unneeded uses cause annoyance or affect comprehension requires a separate user study. Languages and constructions. We study a single Mandarin construction. Although the decision tree is designed to transfer to English it’s not X, it’s Y and other recurring expressions, we have not applied it beyond bushi X, ershi Y . Ethical Considerations This section discusses the ethical considerations and broader impact of this work. Potential Risks. The decision tree describes when a corrective construction is called for, and this description could be used to make model-written text resemble human writing more closely and thus harder to identify. Conversely, the frequency measures could be misread as evidence of machine authorship and applied to judge human writers, who also use the construction. Our analyses concern aggregate usage across models and corpora; they are not designed or validated for attributing individual texts to humans or machines. Intellectual Property. The benchmarks, open-weight checkpoints, reward models, and preference mixtures used in this work are publicly released for research, and we use them in accordance with their respective licenses. Commercial models are accessed through their official APIs under the providers’ terms of service. All materials are used solely for scientific research. Data Privacy. The human reference is drawn from publicly available datasets, and personally identifiable information was removed before analysis. Model answers are generated from public benchmark prompts. The human annotators are students with a background in linguistics who participated voluntarily; no personal information about them is collected beyond their annotations. Intended Use. The diagnostic framework is intended for analyzing contextual appropriateness in model-generated text and for examining how evaluators and training stages shape such usage. It is not intended for authorship detection or for evaluating individual writers. Documentation of Artifacts. We will release our code and the annotation guidelines for the decision tree. Both are documented with respect to their scope: the Mandarin construction bushi X, ershi Y , the task domains covered, and the procedures described in Appendices A – D . AI Assistants in Research or Writing. We use Cursor for code development assistance and a large language model for refining and polishing the language of the paper.
